newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian bonds positive amid the U.S. gloom.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian bonds positive amid the U.S. gloom.

text.p: Australian bond yields ended lower rallying from their initial U.S. led mark-up after today's latest retail trade report.
Although the data pre-dated the December 11 official rate cut, a mere 0.7 percent rise in November retail trade still showed the sector as fairly soft and saw the short-end particularly perky.

"(The data) affirms our view that continuing weak economic and employment growth, in the context of a further improving underlying inflation performance, leaves the door open for another rate cut," said Westpac's senior economist John Peters.
Peters expects a 50 basis points easing from the current official rate of 6.0 percent in the March quarter.
March bill futures broke out of the recent narrow trading range to touch a new contract high of 92.20, pipping the previous 94.19 peak set on the day of the last rate cut.
At the high the contract equates to a cash rate of 5.80 percent at maturity.

With two months of the December quarter now published, retail sales will be hard-pressed to record a positive nominal performance for the quarter even if a large monthly rise is recorded in December, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said in a report.

"With continuing low inflation, if the RBA asks its favourite question in February 'is there room for the economy to grow a little faster without threatening inflation'...the Bank's board may well answer in the affirmative," the report said.
The Reserve Bank is due to hold its monthly board meeting on February 4.

The long-end of the market was perilously close to testing key support in early trading after U.S. Treasuries resumed a weaker trend on Monday on fears of a policy tightening by the Federal Reserve. Those worries are likely to persist in the run-up to Thursday's U.S. PPI and non-farm payrolls on Friday.

The local market outperformed the dollar bloc, spurred on by rumours that a U.S. investment house had recommended switching into Australian debt from Canada. There was also talk of a dual currency issue being put in place. The local yield curve steepened with the long-end stiffled by U.S. concerns.
